methodology: Figures come from the PeakAtlas3D catalog: surveyed elevations and prominence, curated difficulty tiers, best-season windows, permit notes, staging-town distances, trail lists, and OpenStreetMap lodging near each summit. Not live weather, quotas, or prices.

pairs.title: Mt. Whitney vs Mt. Elbert
pairs.query: Which is harder: Mt. Whitney or Mt. Elbert?
pairs.summary: Whitney and Elbert are the two iconic Contiguous U.S. 14ers most hikers compare. Both are high-altitude day objectives when conditions are good, but Whitney’s Portal corridor is permit-regulated in peak season while Elbert is typically a walk-up without a dedicated summit permit. Choose Whitney for the Lower 48 high point and lottery logistics; choose Elbert for a Colorado 14er with simpler access and similar elevation.
pairs.pickA: Pick Whitney if you want the Contiguous U.S. high point, can secure Whitney Portal / Inyo permits, and accept busier trailhead logistics.
pairs.pickB: Pick Elbert if you want ~14,440 ft with a standard Colorado walk-up, no dedicated summit permit, and Leadville-area staging.
pairs.verdict: Elbert is usually the simpler trip; Whitney is the higher-status Lower 48 prize with stricter access rules.

pairs.title: Mt. Rainier vs Mt. Hood
pairs.query: Mt. Rainier or Mt. Hood — which climb should you do?
pairs.summary: Rainier and Hood are the Pacific Northwest volcanoes climbers most often weigh. Rainier is a multi-day glacier expedition with crevasse hazard and climbing permits; Hood is a shorter, steeper snow climb that many parties treat as a long day from Timberline when spring conditions align. Rainier demands more glacier skill and logistics; Hood rewards fitness and early alpine starts with less multi-day overhead.
pairs.pickA: Pick Rainier for a true Cascade glacier expedition, guided or experienced teams, and National Park climbing passes.
pairs.pickB: Pick Hood for a classic spring snow climb closer to Portland with shorter approach and no general summit permit on typical routes.
pairs.verdict: Hood is the quicker Cascade tick; Rainier is the bigger glacier commitment.

pairs.title: Mt. Rainier vs Mt. Shasta
pairs.query: Should I climb Rainier or Shasta?
pairs.summary: Rainier and Shasta are two of the West Coast’s defining glacier volcanoes. Both need snow/ice skills, early starts, and seasonal windows — but Rainier sits in a National Park with climbing pass rules, while Shasta is USFS-managed with summit-pass expectations and California access culture. Compare permit friction, approach length, and how much multi-day glacier travel you want.
pairs.pickA: Pick Rainier for Washington’s iconic park setting, guided glacier routes, and a more expedition-like feel.
pairs.pickB: Pick Shasta for a California Cascade volcano with summit-pass logistics and popular Avalanche Gulch–style snow climbs.
pairs.verdict: Both are serious snow-glacier objectives; Rainier usually means more park bureaucracy, Shasta more California peak-pass planning.

pairs.title: Half Dome vs Mt. Whitney
pairs.query: Half Dome or Whitney — which California classic?
pairs.summary: Half Dome and Whitney are California’s two most searched “bucket list” day objectives. Half Dome is a Yosemite cables scramble when the cables are up — lottery-heavy and shorter in mileage than Whitney but more exposure on the final pitch. Whitney is higher, longer, and regulated through the Whitney Portal corridor. Both need advance planning; neither is a casual walk.
pairs.pickA: Pick Half Dome for Yosemite granite, cables-season drama, and a strenuous scramble day when you hold a cables permit.
pairs.pickB: Pick Whitney for the Contiguous U.S. high point, longer trail mileage, and Inyo / Portal permit logistics.
pairs.verdict: Half Dome is the iconic Yosemite cables day; Whitney is the higher, longer Sierra objective.

pairs.title: Matterhorn vs Mont Blanc
pairs.query: Matterhorn or Mont Blanc — which Alps classic?
pairs.summary: Matterhorn and Mont Blanc are the Alps’ two most famous “name” peaks. Matterhorn is a steep rock-ridge alpine climb (Hörnli and cousins) with hut logistics and technical exposure; Mont Blanc is a high glacier objective with altitude, crevasse hazard, and crowded normal routes. One is a rock pyramid; the other is Western Europe’s high point.
pairs.pickA: Pick Matterhorn for a technical alpine rock ridge above Zermatt with hut-based logistics.
pairs.pickB: Pick Mont Blanc for the Alps high point — glacier travel, altitude, and Chamonix / Courmayeur staging.
pairs.verdict: Matterhorn is the rock icon; Mont Blanc is the altitude and glacier prize.

pairs.title: Matterhorn vs Eiger
pairs.query: Matterhorn vs Eiger — which Swiss alpine climb?
pairs.summary: Matterhorn and Eiger are Switzerland’s most storied alpine walls. Matterhorn’s normal ridges are busy guided rock climbs; Eiger’s reputation is dominated by the Nordwand, though milder routes exist for experienced alpinists. Compare rock-ridge traffic and hut culture (Matterhorn) versus steeper, more committing Bernese Oberland terrain (Eiger).
pairs.pickA: Pick Matterhorn for the classic Hörnli-style rock ridge and Zermatt hut infrastructure.
pairs.pickB: Pick Eiger if you want Bernese Oberland technical alpine climbing and accept a steeper, more committing reputation.
pairs.verdict: Matterhorn is the more guided “classic ridge”; Eiger is the darker technical legend.

pairs.title: Kilimanjaro vs Aconcagua
pairs.query: Kilimanjaro or Aconcagua for a high-altitude trip?
pairs.summary: Kilimanjaro and Aconcagua are the two most compared non-technical high-altitude expeditions. Kili is a guided trek with park fees and operator requirements; Aconcagua is a higher, colder Andean expedition with provincial park permits and more self-supported logistics. Both are about altitude management more than rock climbing.
pairs.pickA: Pick Kilimanjaro for a structured trek with operators, established camps, and African Seven Summits travel.
pairs.pickB: Pick Aconcagua for the Western Hemisphere high point — higher, colder, and more expedition logistics in Mendoza Province.
pairs.verdict: Kilimanjaro is the guided trek; Aconcagua is the higher, harsher expedition.

pairs.title: Longs Peak vs Mt. Elbert
pairs.query: Longs Peak or Elbert for a Colorado 14er?
pairs.summary: Longs and Elbert bookend Colorado 14er difficulty for many day hikers. Elbert is a high walk-up; Longs via the Keyhole is a Class 3 scramble with exposure, earlier starts, and Rocky Mountain National Park access rules. Same state, very different skill and risk profiles.
pairs.pickA: Pick Longs if you are comfortable with Class 3 scrambling, exposure, and RMNP timed-entry / trailhead rules.
pairs.pickB: Pick Elbert for Colorado’s high point as a strenuous hike without technical scrambling on the standard routes.
pairs.verdict: Elbert is the high walk-up; Longs is the technical Front Range classic.

pairs.title: Mt. Fuji vs Mt. Whitney
pairs.summary: Fuji and Whitney are the two most searched “national icon” day hikes across the Pacific. Fuji is a seasonal fee/climb culture with crowded Yoshida and Fujinomiya routes; Whitney is the Contiguous U.S. high point with Portal permits and longer Sierra mileage. Both are Class 1–2 when conditions are good — logistics and culture differ more than technical grade.
pairs.pickA: Pick Fuji for Japan’s icon, summer climbing season fees, and hut-supported overnight or long day culture.
pairs.pickB: Pick Whitney for the Lower 48 high point, Sierra trail mileage, and Inyo permit planning.
pairs.verdict: Similar hike grades on paper; Fuji is seasonal Japanese access culture, Whitney is Sierra permit logistics.

pairs.title: Denali vs Mt. Everest
pairs.summary: Denali and Everest are the expedition extremes people compare when they say “Seven Summits.” Denali is polar, self-reliant glacier travel with NPS registration; Everest is commercial 8000 m logistics with Nepal/China permits and crowded seasons. Both are multi-week commitments far beyond day-hike planning.
pairs.pickA: Pick Denali for Alaska Range expedition skills, cold, and National Park climbing registration.
pairs.pickB: Pick Everest for commercial 8000 m logistics, spring window planning, and the world’s high point.
pairs.verdict: Denali tests polar self-reliance; Everest tests altitude commerce and Himalayan logistics.
